sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Ḥp** (*hp*) — The Bringer of the Flood — belongs to the Egyptian tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Nile, Inundation, Abundance". The name means "The Nile flood god Hapi; from ḥꜥpj"[^1].

ḥp is the Nile flood personified: the annual miracle on which all of Egypt hung, arriving as a blue-green, androgynous, heavy-bellied bringer of plenty. No temple was built to him — he needed none; the river was his temple, and its rising his epiphany.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Ḥp** and serves its temple at [ḥp.com](https://xn--p-xnm.com). The restoration preserves the pharyngeal Ḥ — a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses — which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *hp* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, Griffith Institute, 1962.
D. Bonneau, La Crue du Nil, Librairie C. Klincksieck, Paris, 1964.
Alan H. Gardiner, Egyptian Grammar: Being an Introduction to the Study of Hieroglyphs, Griffith Institute / Oxford University Press (3rd ed. 1957), 1927.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Hieroglyphs as **𓎛𓊪**. Etymologically it means "The Nile flood god Hapi; from ḥꜥpj"[^1].

The ASCII form *hp* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Ḥp** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves the pharyngeal Ḥ — a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses — which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **h** → **Ḥ** — Script-specific diacritic
- **p** → **p** — Same letter

The project holds the domain **ḥp.com** (xn--p-xnm.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, Griffith Institute, 1962.
D. Bonneau, La Crue du Nil, Librairie C. Klincksieck, Paris, 1964.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈħaː.pi/** — Egyptological (from ḥp/ḥꜥpj).[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: HAH-pee; the ḥ is a strong breath, not a plain h.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Egyptian** — ḥp
- **Conventional** — Hapi
- **Greek twin** — Νεῖλος
- **Owned form** — ḥp

ḥp is conventionally vocalized "Hapi"; the ḥ (Gardiner Aa1) is the pharyngeal fricative heard at the start of the name. He must not be confused with Ḥpy the baboon-headed son of Horus — same sound, different god: the restoration keeps the underdot that marks the river-lord's true name.

sources.citation: A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, Griffith Institute, 1962.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name is preserved in Hieroglyphs as **𓎛𓊪**.[^1]

The scholarly transliteration is *ḥp*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- 𓎛 twisted wick of plant fibre = ḥ
- Q3 basket (𓊪) = p
- ḥp is the consonantal skeleton of ḥꜥpj, the Nile inundation god

Written ḥ-p with the water sign and the determinative of the fat-bellied offering-bringer; in the fullest orthographies the name rides in the Hymn to Hapi's papyrus copies. The god himself — blue-skinned, heavy-breasted, crowned with papyrus or lotus — is his own determinative: abundance in human form.

sources.citation: A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, Griffith Institute, 1962.
Alan H. Gardiner, Egyptian Grammar: Being an Introduction to the Study of Hieroglyphs, Griffith Institute / Oxford University Press (3rd ed. 1957), 1927.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
ḥp is the Nile flood personified: the annual miracle on which all of Egypt hung, arriving as a blue-green, androgynous, heavy-bellied bringer of plenty. No temple was built to him — he needed none; the river was his temple, and its rising his epiphany.[^1]

### The Inundation

The akhet season: the river rising to feed the black land — Egypt's single most sacred event.

### The Offerings

He bears trays of fish, fowl, and produce — the land's abundance carried in his own arms.

### The Sema-Tawy

The double Hapi tying papyrus and lotus around the windpipe-sign: the Two Lands knotted into one.

### The Nilometer

His measure at Elephantine: cubits of rise that set the year's tax and the year's hope.

sources.citation: D. Bonneau, La Crue du Nil, Librairie C. Klincksieck, Paris, 1964.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Ḥp concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The blue-green skin** — The water itself, and the vegetation it summons
- **The heavy breasts and belly** — Androgynous abundance — the flood as both father and mother
- **The papyrus and lotus** — Lower and Upper Egypt, both his crowns

sources.citation: A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, Griffith Institute, 1962.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
ḥp has no adventures because he is not a character but an event: the flood. His mythology is hydrology made sacred — the river's rhythm given a face, a hymn, and a table of offerings.[^1]

### The Hymn to Hapi (The Hymn)

The great Hymn to Hapi — a school text for a millennium, surviving in New Kingdom copies — calls him "lord of fish and fowl, maker of barley, creator of wheat," and says what every Egyptian knew: when he is high, the land rejoices; when he fails, "the whole land is in panic." No god in the hymn's Egypt is more feared for absence or praised for arrival.[^2]

### The Tying of the Two Lands (The Union)

On temple thrones across Egypt, two ḥp-figures — one crowned with Upper Egypt's lotus, one with the Delta's papyrus — knot the plants around the sema hieroglyph of the windpipe: sema-tawy, "uniting the Two Lands." The flood itself performs the political theology: one river, one country, one harvest.

### The Caverns of the Nile (The Source)

Egyptians imagined the flood welling from subterranean caverns at the First Cataract — the realm of Khnum at Elephantine — and ḥp dwelling in the abyss with it. The theology matters less than the observation: the river rises at the solstice as Sirius returns, and the whole calendar, tax system, and liturgy bent to his timing.

sources.citation: D. Bonneau, La Crue du Nil, Librairie C. Klincksieck, Paris, 1964.
Alan H. Gardiner, Egyptian Grammar: Being an Introduction to the Study of Hieroglyphs, Griffith Institute / Oxford University Press (3rd ed. 1957), 1927.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
The Greeks called him Neilos and gave the river-god a Greek biography — making him, in some accounts, father of Memphis and ancestor of the Danaid line that returned to Argos. The word "Nile" itself descends through this identification. In Nubia he merged with local flood-lords; in the Fayum, his abundance fed the crocodile cult of Sobek, whose lake was the flood's great reservoir. Every downstream culture read the same rising water and named its own god.[^1]

Within the Egyptian tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[ab|Ꜣb]], [[akh|Ꜣḫ]], [[amun|Ꜣmun]], [[ankh|ꜥnḫ]], [[anubis|Jnpw]], and [[apep|Ꜥpp]].

sources.citation: A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, Griffith Institute, 1962.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: He is the reason Egyptology has a tax-system to study: nilometer readings governed assessments, and the "perfect flood" — about 16 cubits at Memphis — was the single most important number in the ancient economy. The Aswan High Dam ended his annual epiphany in 1970: the fields no longer drown, and Egypt marks the loss in every history of the river. "Hapi" survives in countless modern Egyptian names and in the eco-memory of a regulated Nile.[^1]

sources.citation: A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, Griffith Institute, 1962.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
Nilometers survive at Elephantine (a stairwell of cubit scales rebuilt under the Romans), at Roda island in Cairo (the famous octagonal shaft, Abbasid-era over Fatimid work), and at Philae. His iconography is among the most common in Egyptian art: the procession of fat-bellied offering-bringers lines the base of temple walls from Karnak to Dendera, and the double-ḥp sema-tawy decorates royal thrones from the Old Kingdom onward. The Hymn to Hapi's best copies come from school texts — pupils learned the river's praise by heart.[^1]

He had no temple of his own — the river was his sanctuary — but his stations survive as engineering: the **nilometers** of **Elephantine**, where a stairwell of cubit-scales measured his rising beside Khnum's temple; **Philae**, where the flood's arrival was met with festivals at Isis' island; and the **Roda nilometer** in Cairo, whose Abbasid shaft still descends to the river. His iconography lines the base of every temple wall — the long processions of offering-bringers, each a province's flood personified — so that to walk around an Egyptian temple is to watch ḥp feed the country, province by province, forever.

sources.citation: A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, Griffith Institute, 1962.
Bonneau, La Crue du Nil; the Elephantine and Roda nilometer publications.

sections.label: Hieroglyphic Evidence
sections.body:
The flood's titles are the names of abundance itself.

- **ꜥꜣ-pḥty** — 'great of might'; the flood's force acknowledged.
- **nb-t3wy** — 'lord of the Two Lands'; the river that is the country's unity.
- **jtw-nṯrw** — 'father of the gods'; the inundation as the oldest giver.
- **ḥp** — 'the hidden one', on one ancient reading: the flood whose source no one has seen.
- **di-ꜥnḫ** — 'giver of life'; the standing doxology of the hymns.
- **ḥqꜣ-ʿḥ** — 'ruler of the field'; the harvest's true landlord.

sources.citation: The Hymn to Hapi (van der Plas, L'Hymne à la Crue du Nil).

sections.label: Pyramid Texts
sections.body: The Pyramid Texts address the flood constantly, if the god by name more rarely: utterances summon the inundation for the king's provisioning — "the waters of life that are in the sky, the waters of life that are in the earth" — and the king is nourished by the flood's abundance. ḥp as a personified bringer crystallizes later, but the pyramid liturgy already treats the Nile's rise as a divine event addressed directly. The oldest corpus thus knows his substance: the year's life arrives on water, and someone must be thanked.

sources.citation: Faulkner, Pyramid Texts (inundation utterances).

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Coffin Texts
sections.body: The Coffin Texts give the flood its full provisioning role for the common dead: spells promise the inundation's food and drink in the Field of Reeds, and the deceased is identified with the flood's own abundance — "I am Hapi" in the formula's logic, the provisioner and the provisioned one. The Middle Kingdom's theology of the afterlife as a well-watered Egypt perfected makes the flood-god the ferryman of sustenance itself, and the spells' water-supply clauses are his everyday liturgy.

sources.citation: Faulkner, Coffin Texts (provisioning spells).

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Book of the Dead
sections.body: In the Book of the Dead, water is survival: spells "for bringing air and water in the god's domain" and for drinking in the necropolis invoke the flood's generosity by name and function. The vignettes of the justified dead ploughing and reaping in the Field of Reeds show his afterlife version — an Egypt of perfect inundation. And the **Hymn to Hapi**, though a separate composition, circulated in the same school milieu: New Kingdom pupils learned both the spells of the dead and the praise of the river that feeds the living.

sources.citation: Book of the Dead (water spells); the Hymn to Hapi (van der Plas).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
ḥp is the god of the right amount. Too little and Egypt starved; too much and it drowned: his theology is the arithmetic of enough. Every flood-forecast, every reservoir, every rationing scheme since is his liturgy translated — the oldest question of abundance is not how to get more, but how to receive what comes.

The dam ended his flood in a single generation, and Egypt's ambivalence about the Aswan High Dam is his modern myth: the silt no longer comes, the fields are fed by chemistry, the delta retreats — and no one would vote to bring the drowning back. ḥp's question outlives his river: abundance engineered is abundance owed to what? The flood that fed for five thousand years was never free; it was merely invoiced in a currency — rhythm, silt, patience — that modernity is only now learning to price again.

The hymn says it plainly: when he rises, the land rejoices; when he fails, the temples themselves seem to close. Egypt knew what every river civilization relearns — the water is not a resource but a relationship, renewed annually or not at all. The nilometer's cubits were the oldest economic forecast in the world, and the tax register waited on the river like a priest on an oracle.[^1]

sources.citation: A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, Griffith Institute, 1962.
